title: Blackening a name vs. burnishing one
core: Every word here moves a reputation — not a person's feelings, but how third parties rate them. Six push the standing down through damaging speech; four push it up through praise, reverence, or official blessing. They blur because English sorts them on axes the definitions don't announce: whether the claim must be *false*, whether it's *spoken or published*, whether it's *stated or merely hinted*, whether *one person or a crowd or an institution* is doing it, and whether the word's disapproval falls on the target or on the speaker.
exam_note: The trap is treating the six negatives as interchangeable: only **defame**, **slander** and **calumny** require the claim to be false, while **denigrate** and **malign** need only be unfair — and on the positive side the exam swaps a felt reverence (**venerate**) for a public fuss (**lionize**) or an institutional ruling (**canonize**).

words.nuance: The only pure noun for the *lie itself* rather than the act or the law. **Calumny** convicts the accuser of malice — using it means you have already sided with the victim — whereas *defamation* and *slander* stay neutral until a court rules.

Nothing is actually alleged. **Aspersions** are insinuations, plural and sidelong, usually smuggled in by the person disavowing them ("I cast no aspersions on his honesty"); a slander can be denied point by point, an aspersion has no point to deny.

The umbrella verb of the tort, covering both written *libel* and spoken *slander*. It demands two things the softer words don't: the statement must be false, and it must reach an audience — a truthful exposé defames nobody, and neither does a private sneer.

**Defame**'s spoken half, and the strictest word here: the claim must be oral, false, and dressed as fact. "My boss is an idiot" is opinion and safe; "my boss embezzled" is slander. Also the group's only member with a plain neutral register.

No falsehood needed — you can **denigrate** with true facts by dwelling on them out of all proportion. It attacks worth rather than conduct, works on things as well as people (a book, a rival's achievements), and reads as a sustained campaign of talking-down, not a single published charge.

Ill-speaking done behind the back, with no legal apparatus attached and no volume required — unlike **defame** or **slander**, nobody sues over it. Its signature is the passive: *a much-maligned* X almost always means the victim didn't deserve it.

The pivot to the positive side, and the only word here whose object is the reputation rather than the person — and often your own. You can **burnish** only what already exists, and the figurative use hints at PR: shine applied to the surface, nothing changed underneath.

A crowd's doing — critics, salons, the lecture circuit — and it describes the fuss, not the merit. Where **venerate** is hushed and **canonize** is permanent, lionizing is noisy, fashionable and revocable; writers use it to hint the adulation outran the work.

Reverence felt, not performance staged: one notch below worship, owed to age, holiness, the honoured dead. **Lionize** parades the living; **venerate** looks upward and usually backward, placing its object above ordinary criticism — which is exactly the implication a critic exploits.

Not a feeling but a ruling — the Church, the academy, the syllabus. **Lionizing** a figure can go out of fashion next season; **canonizing** freezes the reputation and puts it past debate, which is why the word turns dry the moment the honour is undeserved.
